scrambled-egg-tomato-toast.text:
About this meal: Using extra egg whites strengthens the protein content without needing another yolk, which brings considerably more phosphate. That is a useful compromise when protein and phosphate both need attention.

Protein: The combination of whole egg and egg white supplies protein while limiting how many yolks the recipe uses. Whites and yolks are not nutritionally interchangeable, so replacing the extra whites with another whole egg would also change the phosphorus and fat balance.

Carbohydrates: The starch-containing ingredients here include white bread. Use the exact dry, raw or cooked amount specified. Cooking changes how much water a food holds, so equal weights before and after cooking do not necessarily represent the same carbohydrate portion. Use the carbohydrate figure rather than only the “of which sugars” line when checking a UK product label; fibre is listed separately. Any extra toast, rice, fruit or sweetened drink needs counting separately.

Fibre and balance: Fibre comes from white bread. If changing the dish to manage one mineral or carbohydrate, consider what else the swap removes: replacing a pulse or wholegrain with a more refined starch changes fibre as well as the nutrient you were targeting. Choose the trade-off against the whole day.

Potassium: Ingredients including tomato contribute potassium as well as useful food value. If potassium is restricted for you, consider the portion and the other meals that day before removing whole food groups. A small measured ingredient need not determine the suitability of the whole meal.

Phosphorus: Natural phosphorus comes from ingredients such as egg and liquid egg whites. Manage this with the serving and the rest of the day rather than assuming that every food in a protein-rich group has the same effect. Check processed versions and substitutes for ingredients containing “phos”, especially when changing the specified product; additives may change the balance.

Salt and flavour: Compare the labels on white bread when choosing products for this recipe. Their sodium content can vary, and a product that sounds similar may not match the one used in the calculation. Keep any sauces or seasoning to the listed amounts rather than adding them freely at the table.

Energy and fats: Richness and energy come partly from butter, alongside a saturated-fat contribution. Increasing these ingredients to make the meal more substantial changes more than just its texture. Compare the whole serving with your energy needs rather than judging it only by the size of the main ingredient.

Cooking and adaptations: Use the preparation and doneness checks in the method, with separate utensils for raw and ready-to-eat food. Keep the specified cooking fats and edible sauce within the serving; extra marinades or a different cut of meat can change the nutrient balance even when the finished dish looks similar.

Ingredient checks: This version includes ingredients flagged for wheat or other gluten-containing cereals, egg, milk. Check actual packet labels, including compound ingredients and cross-contact information. A vegan, vegetarian or low-FODMAP category is not an allergen-free claim; replacing an ingredient also changes the recipe calculation.

Extra oil, sauce or topping is part of what you eat and needs including in any revised calculation.
